label: Chapter 3: Capital of the Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands, 1430 to 1568

units.text: In 1430, Brussels hit the jackpot.
The duchy of Brabant passed to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, one of the richest and most glamorous princes in Europe.
And Philip made a choice that changed the city's destiny.
Out of all his great towns, he chose Brussels as his main residence.
To understand why that mattered, you need to picture the Burgundian state.
It was not a kingdom on a map the way we think of kingdoms.

It was a patchwork of territories collected through marriage, inheritance, and purchase: Flanders, Brabant, Holland, Hainaut, and soon the duchy of Luxembourg, which Philip took in 1443, as we heard in the story of Luxembourg.
These territories covered roughly what is now Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg, and a good slice of northern France.
Philip ruled them from a court that was the most dazzling in Europe, full of knights, painters, musicians, and diplomats.
In 1430, the same year he inherited Brabant, he founded a famous chivalric brotherhood, the Order of the Golden Fleece.
And the heart of that court, more and more, was Brussels.
The dukes lived at the Coudenberg Palace, on the hill above the town, which they enlarged into a huge complex of halls, chapels, and courtyards.
Government offices followed the court.
Money followed the offices. Artists and craftsmen followed the money.
The art of this period is extraordinary.
In 1436, the city appointed a painter named Rogier van der Weyden as its official city painter.
Rogier, who had been born in Tournai and trained there, became one of the great masters of what we now call Early Netherlandish painting.
His portraits, with their sharp, searching faces, and his emotional religious scenes, were admired across Europe.
For the town hall, he painted a series of panels about justice, scenes of rulers hearing the cases of ordinary people.
Those paintings were destroyed in 1695, but the artist's reputation lived on.
Rogier is buried in the cathedral of Brussels.
Brussels also became famous for tapestry.
Weavers in the city produced huge, richly colored wall hangings, made of wool, silk, and threads of gold and silver.
Tapestries were the luxury art of the age, and a prince would pay more for a fine set than for a painting.

Brussels workshops became so renowned that, in the 1510s, Pope Leo the Tenth commissioned a set of tapestries for the Sistine Chapel, based on designs by Raphael, and the weaving was done in Brussels.
The city soon introduced a quality mark, a pair of the letter B around a red shield, woven into the edge of authentic pieces to protect the brand.
The Burgundian dream ended abruptly in 1477.
Philip's grandson, Charles the Bold, was killed fighting the Swiss and Lorrainers outside the city of Nancy, leaving a single daughter, Mary of Burgundy.
Mary had been born in Brussels, and she was the most eligible heiress in Europe.
She married Maximilian of Habsburg, an Austrian prince who would become Holy Roman Emperor, and when she died in a riding accident in 1482, her lands passed to their children.
Through that marriage, the Burgundian Netherlands fell into the hands of the Habsburgs, the most powerful dynasty of the next three centuries.
The most important Habsburg for Brussels was Mary's grandson, Charles.
He was born in Ghent in the year 1500, but he was raised in the Netherlands and he saw Brussels as home.
When he was six, he inherited the Burgundian lands, and in 1516, he was proclaimed King of Spain in a ceremony in the church of Saint Gudula in Brussels.
In 1519, he was elected Holy Roman Emperor, as Charles the Fifth, ruler of an empire that stretched from Spain and Italy to Germany, the Netherlands, and the new Spanish colonies in the Americas.
Charles was usually traveling, so he needed trusted regents to govern the Netherlands in his absence.
His aunt Margaret of Austria ruled from nearby Mechelen.
Later, his sister Mary of Hungary took over, and in 1531 the central government institutions were fixed in Brussels.
That is when Brussels truly became the capital of the Low Countries, a role it has kept, in one form or another, ever since.
It was also a time of intellectual brilliance.

In 1521, the great humanist Erasmus of Rotterdam, the most famous scholar in Europe, spent several months in Anderlecht, then a village outside Brussels, living in a house that you can visit today as a museum.
In 1514, a boy named Andreas Vesalius was born in Brussels.
He grew up to be a pioneer of modern anatomy, and his groundbreaking book on the structure of the human body, published in 1543, corrected centuries of errors by examining real corpses.
And in 1563, the great painter Pieter Bruegel the Elder moved to Brussels.
He married the daughter of a well-known local artist, and in the remaining years of his short life he painted some of his most famous scenes of peasant life and village feasts.
He died in Brussels in 1569 and was buried in a church in the Marolles district.
Charles made one more big mark on the city.
In 1549, there was a great festival in Brussels to present his son and heir, Philip, to the people of the Netherlands.
The procession of guilds, nobles, and giant figures that wound through the streets is remembered today in a summer pageant called the Ommegang, held every year on the Grand Place.
And in October of 1555, in the great hall of the Coudenberg Palace, Charles gave up his crown.
Exhausted, ill, and weary of rule, he announced that he was handing the Netherlands over to Philip the Second.
Witnesses recorded that he leaned on the shoulder of a young nobleman, the twenty-two-year-old William of Orange, and that the hall wept as he spoke.
Soon afterward, he handed Spain over too, and retired to a monastery.
By now, Brussels was a city of tens of thousands of people, a great center of government, art, and trade.
But dark clouds were on the horizon.
In 1517, a German monk named Martin Luther had challenged the Catholic Church, and the new Protestant ideas spread quickly through the Low Countries.
In 1523, in the very center of Brussels, two young Augustinian monks, Henry Voes and Johannes van den Esschen, were burned at the stake on the Grand Place for refusing to renounce Luther's teachings.
They are considered the first martyrs of the Protestant Reformation.
It was a sign of things to come.
Philip the Second, the new ruler, was a devoutly Catholic king who lived in Spain and never really understood the Netherlands.
He intended to stamp out heresy, enforce Catholic orthodoxy, and tighten royal control over the proud cities.
The cities, with their ancient privileges, were not going to give in without a fight.
If you want to touch this chapter, go to the Place Royale, at the top of the hill.
Under the square, an archaeological site called the Coudenberg lets you walk through the surviving cellars and streets of the old ducal palace.
You will be walking the same ground where Charles the Fifth gave up the biggest empire in the world.
In the next chapter, revolt, execution, bombardment, and an elegant rebuilding.
